description: Argument, inference, validity, evidence, burden of proof, rhetoric, debate, and the razors, each in four layers.

depth.picture: A claim together with the reasons offered for it, set out so that anyone can see what is being asked of them and check each step.
depth.mechanism: You state a conclusion, give premises that are supposed to support it, and rely on an inference linking the two. A listener can accept or reject the premises, or accept the premises and reject the link.
depth.detail: Every argument can be pulled apart the same way: identify the conclusion, list the premises, note any premise left unstated, and ask two separate questions. Are the premises true? Does the conclusion actually follow? Arguments come in two broad kinds: deductive, where the premises are meant to guarantee the conclusion, and inductive, where they only make it likely. Most real-life arguments are inductive, and many depend on an unstated premise that is the real point of dispute.
depth.principles: An argument is a way of making thinking public. Because each step is exposed, others can find the weak one, and so can you. That is why arguing well is a cooperative act: the aim is to find out what is true together, not to defeat someone.

depth.picture: Reasoning in which the conclusion is forced: if the starting points are true, the conclusion cannot possibly be false.
depth.mechanism: You start from premises and apply rules that only ever rearrange what is already there. Because nothing new is added, nothing can go wrong in the step itself; any error must lie in the premises.
depth.detail: Classic forms include the syllogism (all A are B; all B are C; so all A are C), modus ponens (if P then Q; P; so Q) and modus tollens (if P then Q; not Q; so not P). Mathematics is built almost entirely from deduction. Its strength is certainty; its limit is that the conclusion is already contained in the premises, so deduction clarifies what you know but does not by itself discover new facts about the world.
depth.principles: Deduction is truth-preserving: it carries truth from premises to conclusion without loss, but cannot create it. That is why it is paired with induction and abduction, which take the risk of going beyond what was given.

depth.picture: Reasoning from things you have seen to something more general, or to something you have not seen yet: the sun has risen every day so far, so it will rise tomorrow.
depth.mechanism: You gather cases, notice a pattern, and project it beyond the cases observed. The more numerous and varied the cases, the more confident you can be, but no number of cases can make the conclusion certain.
depth.detail: Forms include generalization from a sample, prediction from past regularity, and reasoning by analogy. Its strength depends on sample size, how representative the sample is, and whether the underlying process is stable. It underlies science, medicine, and everyday learning. The classic difficulty, Hume's problem of induction, is that there is no non-circular way to prove the future will resemble the past. Statistics is largely the discipline of doing induction carefully.
depth.principles: Induction is ampliative: it adds content beyond the premises, and that is exactly why it can be wrong. Knowledge that grows must take that risk; deduction is safe because it never goes anywhere new. Good inductive reasoning is about sizing the risk honestly.

depth.picture: Inference to the best explanation: you see something surprising and ask what would make it unsurprising.
depth.mechanism: From an observation you generate candidate explanations, compare how well each accounts for the facts and how few extra assumptions it needs, and provisionally accept the best. The choice stays open to revision.
depth.detail: A doctor reasons from symptoms to a diagnosis; a detective from clues to a suspect; a scientist from an anomaly to a hypothesis. The philosopher Charles Peirce named it, distinguishing it from deduction and induction. Criteria for a good explanation include how much it explains, how simple it is, how well it fits everything else we know, and whether it makes testable predictions. Abduction proposes; deduction and induction then test.
depth.principles: Deduction cannot generate a hypothesis and induction can only extend one; abduction is where hypotheses come from. It is fallible because more than one explanation can fit, and the best available may still be wrong, so it is a starting point for testing rather than a conclusion.

depth.picture: An argument is valid when its shape guarantees the conclusion: there is no way for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.
depth.mechanism: You ignore what the argument is about and look only at its form. If every way of filling in the blanks that makes the premises true also makes the conclusion true, the form is valid.
depth.detail: Validity is a property of the form, not of the content. All cats are planets; all planets are made of cheese; so all cats are made of cheese is valid, though its premises are absurd. A test is to imagine a case where the premises hold and the conclusion fails: if you can, the argument is invalid. Truth tables and Venn diagrams are systematic ways to run that test.
depth.principles: Separating form from content is what makes logic powerful. It lets us check reasoning without knowing the subject, and it shows that a good argument needs two things: good form, and true premises. Validity alone gets you only halfway.

depth.picture: A sound argument is one that is both valid and has true premises, which is what you need before its conclusion can be trusted.
depth.mechanism: First check the form: does the conclusion follow? Then check each premise against the world. Only if both pass is the conclusion guaranteed to be true.
depth.detail: An argument can fail in two independent ways: it can be invalid, with a form that does not guarantee the conclusion, or unsound despite being valid, because at least one premise is false. Debates often go wrong by confusing the two: a person may attack the form when the real weakness is a premise, or the reverse. Logicians reserve the word sound for arguments that pass both tests.
depth.principles: Truth and validity are different virtues, and only together do they deliver truth. This is why disputes so often come down to premises: logic can tell you what follows, but only evidence about the world can tell you whether to start from there.

depth.picture: Anything that makes a claim more or less likely to be true.
depth.mechanism: Evidence works by discriminating: an observation is good evidence for a claim to the extent it would be much more likely if the claim were true than if it were false. The bigger the difference, the stronger the evidence.
depth.detail: Ways to weigh it include how directly it bears on the claim, how reliable the source is, whether it was gathered to test the claim or to confirm it, whether it can be checked independently, and whether other explanations account for it equally well. Kinds include direct observation, measurement, testimony, documents, and statistical patterns. In Bayesian terms, evidence updates a prior belief into a posterior one by an amount set by how strongly it favors one hypothesis over another.
depth.principles: Evidence is not proof; it is a matter of degree. Good thinking means holding beliefs in proportion to the evidence and being willing to change them when evidence changes, which requires knowing what would count against your view as well as for it.

depth.picture: Whoever makes a claim owes the reasons for it; those who doubt it owe nothing until they have been given some.
depth.mechanism: In a dispute, the person asserting something takes on the job of supporting it. If they do not, the claim can be set aside without any counter-evidence, because a bare assertion has done nothing to earn belief.
depth.detail: In law the burden usually falls on the prosecution, and its weight varies: beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases, balance of probabilities in civil ones. In everyday and scientific argument, the burden grows with how surprising the claim is. Trying to shift it, by demanding others disprove a claim, is the appeal to ignorance. The burden can also shift back once one side has offered credible support.
depth.principles: The rule exists because claims are cheap and disproof is expensive: nearly anything can be asserted, and nobody can refute everything. Placing the burden on the claimant keeps discussion from being flooded by unsupported assertions.

depth.picture: Restating your opponent's view in the strongest form you can, so that if you still disagree, you are disagreeing with the best version of it.
depth.mechanism: Before replying, you rebuild their argument: fill in unstated premises, drop weak examples, add better ones, and state it so well that they would say yes, that is what I meant. Only then do you respond.
depth.detail: It is the deliberate opposite of a straw man. A common form is to ask, what is the best reason someone might hold this? Some traditions ask you to state the other side to their satisfaction before you may criticize it. Steelmanning does not mean agreeing, and it can fail if you invent a stronger position than the person actually holds; the aim is to be fair, not to argue against yourself.
depth.principles: Winning against a weak version teaches you nothing, and convinces only people who already agree. Beating the strongest version, or finding it persuades you, is the only way to learn. It is intellectual honesty put into practice.

depth.picture: Interpret what someone says in the most reasonable and sensible way you can, until you have good reason not to.
depth.mechanism: When a statement could be read as foolish or as sensible, assume the sensible reading. You give the speaker the benefit of the doubt about their competence and good faith.
depth.detail: Philosophers such as Donald Davidson made it central to understanding other people: without assuming most of what others say is rational and true, interpretation cannot get started. In debate it means responding to what was probably meant, not the most literal or worst reading. It has limits: it does not require ignoring real contradictions, nor believing that a person cannot have been wrong.
depth.principles: Communication depends on cooperation. Reading charitably keeps conversation productive, and gives you a better chance of learning something, because the most plausible reading of a thoughtful person is usually the one that has something in it.

depth.picture: The classic three-line argument: All humans are mortal. Socrates is human. So Socrates is mortal.
depth.mechanism: Two premises share a middle term (human here). The first relates the middle term to one category, the second places something in the middle term, and the conclusion links the two ends.
depth.detail: Aristotle catalogued the valid forms, called moods, by whether each statement is universal or particular, and affirmative or negative: for example, All M are P, all S are M, so all S are P. Medieval logicians memorized them with mnemonic names. Venn diagrams offer a quick check: shade the premises and see whether the conclusion is already shaded. Common errors include the undistributed middle and drawing a conclusion stronger than the premises allow.
depth.principles: The syllogism shows that valid reasoning depends on how categories nest inside one another, not on what the categories are. It is the first formal system of logic, and set theory later revealed its simple structure: containment is transitive.

depth.picture: If P then Q. P. Therefore Q. The most basic valid step in reasoning.
depth.mechanism: You hold a rule that says one thing leads to another, and you know the first thing is true. So you may conclude the second.
depth.detail: Example: if it is raining, the ground is wet; it is raining; so the ground is wet. Latin for mode that affirms. It is the engine of rule-based systems: a program that checks a condition and then acts, or a proof that applies a theorem to a case, is doing modus ponens. Its cousin, affirming the consequent (Q, therefore P), looks similar but is invalid.
depth.principles: It is valid because the conditional excludes exactly one situation: P true and Q false. Once P is known true, that situation is ruled out and Q is all that remains. Nearly all logical systems either take it as a basic rule or can derive it.

depth.picture: If P then Q. Not Q. Therefore not P. If the consequence didn't happen, the cause can't have been there.
depth.mechanism: You hold a rule saying P leads to Q, and you observe that Q did not occur. Since P would have produced Q, P must be false.
depth.detail: Example: if the suspect were here, his coat would be on the hook; it is not; so he is not here. Scientists use it to test theories: a theory predicts an outcome; if the outcome fails to occur, the theory (or an assumption behind it) is in trouble. Its invalid cousin is denying the antecedent (not P, therefore not Q).
depth.principles: It is the logical core of falsification. Because a single failed prediction can refute a claim whereas any number of successes cannot prove it, modus tollens gives science its asymmetry between confirming and refuting.

depth.picture: Patterns of bad reasoning that feel convincing, catalogued so they can be recognized.
depth.mechanism: Each fallacy is a recurring way an argument fails to support its conclusion: through bad form, irrelevance, hidden assumptions, misused evidence, or a quirk of human judgment. Naming a pattern lets you spot it faster.
depth.detail: Formal fallacies are wrong by their structure alone (like affirming the consequent). Informal fallacies fail through content or context: relevance (straw man, ad hominem), presumption (begging the question, false dilemma), causation (post hoc), evidence (hasty generalization), and appeals to non-reasons (authority, popularity). Behind many sit cognitive biases. Fallacies are best used on your own reasoning first, and with care on others, since calling one is not a refutation.
depth.principles: Fallacies persist because they exploit shortcuts that usually serve us well. A conclusion can still be true when the argument for it is fallacious, so pointing to a fallacy shows only that the argument fails, not that the claim is false.

depth.picture: The art of persuading with words, studied since ancient Greece.
depth.mechanism: A speaker fits the message to the audience and the moment: establishing credibility, arranging the points, choosing language, and touching feeling, so that the argument lands and is remembered.
depth.detail: Classical rhetoric had five parts: inventing arguments, arranging them, styling them, memorizing, and delivering. Aristotle named three appeals (ethos, pathos, logos) and three occasions: courtroom, political assembly, and ceremony. Figures of speech (metaphor, repetition, contrast, the rule of three) shape how words feel. Rhetoric is often used to mean empty talk, but it is simply the study of how language moves people.
depth.principles: Persuasion works on people, not on abstractions, so even sound arguments need to be delivered well to be heard. The same skills serve honesty and deception alike, which is why learning them is a defense as well as a craft.

depth.picture: Aristotle's three ways to convince: trust the speaker (ethos), feel something (pathos), or follow the reasoning (logos).
depth.mechanism: Ethos persuades through character and credibility; pathos through the emotions of the audience; logos through the argument. A speaker blends them, and audiences respond to all three at once.
depth.detail: Ethos is built by showing knowledge, good sense, and goodwill. Pathos includes fear, hope, anger, and pity, and is legitimate when the emotion suits the facts. Logos is evidence and logical structure. Manipulation often leans on one appeal alone, such as pathos without logos or ethos borrowed from unrelated fame. Later writers added kairos, the fitness of the moment.
depth.principles: Humans are not purely rational, so a message that ignores credibility and feeling is likely to fail even when correct. The ethical test is whether the appeals are honest and proportionate: are they helping people see the truth, or bypassing their judgment?

depth.picture: Testing and teaching ideas by asking questions, so the answerer finds their own mistakes.
depth.mechanism: A questioner asks a person to state a belief, then asks follow-ups that draw out its consequences. When these clash with something else the person holds, a contradiction appears and the belief must be refined.
depth.detail: Named for Socrates as portrayed in Plato's dialogues, which often end in puzzlement rather than an answer. Modern uses include law school classes (questioning students about cases), therapy and coaching, and code reviews. Typical questions: what do you mean by that? what follows from it? what is an example? what would count against it? Done badly it becomes interrogation; done well it is a shared inquiry.
depth.principles: People learn more from discovering an inconsistency themselves than from being told. Questions expose hidden assumptions without asserting a rival view, which is why the method works as both a way to teach and a way to find out what you really think.

depth.picture: Reaching a better idea through the collision of opposing ones, keeping what was right on both sides.
depth.mechanism: A view (thesis) is challenged by its opposite (antithesis). Rather than one simply winning, the tension is resolved by a richer view (synthesis) that preserves the truth in each. The synthesis then becomes the next thesis.
depth.detail: The word covers several traditions: Socratic dialogue by question and answer; Hegel's triad of thesis, antithesis, synthesis (often attributed to him, though he used other terms); and Marx's materialist version applied to history. In everyday use it describes any conversation where opposing positions are used to refine each other rather than just to defeat each other.
depth.principles: Contradictions are a source of progress, not only error: pressure from an opposite exposes what a view leaves out. It also gives a shape to disagreement in which each side is useful to the other.

depth.picture: Arguing against a position, even one you hold, in order to test it.
depth.mechanism: One person takes the opposing side on purpose and presses the strongest objections. The group hears the counterarguments before committing, and weaknesses show while they are still cheap to fix.
depth.detail: The term comes from the Catholic Church's role of the advocatus diaboli, who argued against the canonization of a candidate. Organizations use the same idea in pre-mortems, red teams, and review boards. It is most useful when the advocate is clearly playing a role, so that criticism is not taken as personal, and when the group is at risk of groupthink.
depth.principles: Groups tend to agree too quickly, and individuals tend to look only for support. Assigning someone the job of disagreement counters both, and separates a good idea from the wish that it be true.

depth.picture: A structured contest of arguments over a proposition, with a way to judge which case was made better.
depth.mechanism: Two sides are assigned a motion and given fixed turns to speak, respond, and close. Judges or an audience weigh how well each case was reasoned, supported, and answered, often regardless of what they believed beforehand.
depth.detail: Formats vary: parliamentary, policy, Lincoln–Douglas, public forum, and moot court. Debaters are often assigned a side they do not hold, which builds the habit of understanding opposing views. Typical elements are a case with a few contentions, rebuttal, cross-examination, and a closing. Good debate rewards clarity, evidence, and directly answering the other side.
depth.principles: Adversarial testing is a powerful way to find weaknesses, and the discipline of arguing either side separates the quality of an argument from the loyalty of the arguer. It works best when it serves understanding rather than victory, since winning a debate does not make a claim true.

depth.picture: When two explanations fit the facts equally well, prefer the one that assumes less.
depth.mechanism: Every extra assumption is another thing that could be wrong, and another thing you have not tested. Cutting unneeded ones leaves an explanation that is easier to check and less likely to be fitted to the noise.
depth.detail: Attributed to the fourteenth-century friar William of Ockham: entities are not to be multiplied beyond necessity. It is a heuristic, not a law: the simplest explanation is not always right, and simple is not the same as familiar. Its modern forms include model selection in statistics (penalizing complexity) and the minimum description length principle, which links it to compression.
depth.principles: Simpler theories generalize better because they have fewer places to overfit accidental features of the data. The razor is a bet about where to look first, justified by how often it pays off, not a guarantee about the universe.

depth.picture: Don't assume malice when carelessness or ignorance would explain it just as well.
depth.mechanism: When someone harms you or acts badly, consider first the boring explanations: they didn't know, were rushed, or made a mistake. Only when those fail do you consider intent.
depth.detail: Named after Robert Hanlon, though the sentiment is older. It corrects a bias in which we read others' behavior as intentional and about us. It is a probability judgment: stupidity, error, and misunderstanding are far more common than scheming. It does not excuse harm, and real malice does exist; it only sets the order of your guesses.
depth.principles: Assuming bad intent escalates conflict and is usually wrong. Assuming an honest mistake keeps a conversation open, lets the other person correct course without losing face, and matches the actual frequencies of human behavior.

depth.picture: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence: the stranger the claim, the stronger the proof needed.
depth.mechanism: A claim that conflicts with a lot of well-established knowledge starts with a very low prior probability. Ordinary evidence, which could easily arise from error or fraud, is not enough to overcome it.
depth.detail: Popularized by Carl Sagan, echoing earlier statements by Laplace and Hume (a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence). In Bayesian terms, posterior odds equal prior odds times the strength of the evidence; a tiny prior needs an enormous likelihood ratio. Extraordinary claims sometimes turn out true, which is why the standard asks for strong evidence rather than refusal.
depth.principles: The reliability of evidence must be weighed against how likely the alternative explanations are. A surprising report is more likely to be a mistake, a hoax, or a misreading than a discovery, until the evidence rules those out.

depth.picture: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.
depth.mechanism: If someone offers a claim with no support, you owe it no counter-argument. Until reasons are given there is nothing to rebut, and you may simply decline to accept it.
depth.detail: Named after Christopher Hitchens, who stated it in the 2000s, and related to a much older Latin maxim. It is the burden of proof turned into a rule of thumb. It applies to bare assertions, not to claims that have been supported: once evidence is offered, it has to be engaged with. It can be misused as a way to wave away any view one dislikes.
depth.principles: Without it, anyone could force others to disprove any statement, which is impossible. Requiring support from whoever makes a claim keeps the work where the knowledge is, and keeps inquiry from being swamped by unsupported assertions.
